If the penult does not have a long vowel stress is on the final syllable if it has a high tone. If both are not the case, stress is on the first syllable. ... [Downing 2004:108] Iraqw, a South Cushitic language spoken in Tanzania, is described as having a very different sort of accent system, with quantity-sensitive stress, as well as tone (Mous 1993). High tones pattern with long vowels in attracting stress. ... the penult is stressed if it has a long vowel. If the penult has a short vowel and the final syllable has a High tone, then the final syllable is stressed. Otherwise, the first syllable is stressed. sweep_summary: this search of works with stress in the title listed one title for Iraqw, Downing 2004 (ZASPiL 37); its glottolog URL is dead but the official OJS copy (DOI 10.21248/zaspil.37.2004.247) was downloaded and is byte-identical to the copy already in custody; p.108 paraphrases Mous 1993's three-clause rule (long penult > final H > initial) with Mous's examples, confirming the catalog's quoted carrier. Chasing the works still to obtain Kiessling 2004 found an open author preprint (publisher-permitted) plus Kiessling 2000; Kiessling 2004 preprint p.4 quotes Mous 1993:23 verbatim with locator and states first-hand that Iraqw tone is independent of stress, that stress is predictable (accent-1 words: last heavy syllable, antepenult or penult; accent 2: terminal H), and (fn.5) that Alagwa/Burunge differ. This is the best statement read this search of works with stress in the title: it refines the catalog's 'conflict' coding by showing the Mous-vs-Maghway disagreement is terminological, without superseding Mous 1993 as primary. Mous 1993 itself (p. Mous 2020 OHAL is paywalled. Six new files and a manifest Custody note: the held Mous 2007 sketch in was downloaded by an earlier reading from a site we do not cite; it was not used here.

new_statements.quote: In Iraqw, tone is independent of vowel length and of stress. [...] Stress on the other hand "is predictable on the basis of the syllable structure and the tone. Stress is on the penultimate syllable if this syllable contains a long vowel. If the penultimate syllable has a short vowel, stress is on the last syllable, if this syllable has a high tone and otherwise on the first syllable." (Mous 1993: 23).

new_statements.reading: A first-hand West Rift specialist states that Iraqw stress is a predictable, non-contrastive prominence separate from the H/L pitch accent, and reproduces Mous 1993:23 verbatim with its page: penult if it has a long vowel; otherwise final if it carries H tone; otherwise initial. His own reformulation (preprint p.3) puts accent-1 stress on the last heavy syllable of the phonological word (antepenult or penult) with accent-2 prominence on the terminal H syllable, which coincides with Mous's clauses for two- and three-syllable words. Together with Downing 2004:108 and the StressTyp2 entrythis makes three carriers of the identical Mous sentence, one of them a direct quotation with locator by an independent specialist. It does not supply a competing position, so it supports the Mous side of the catalog's 'conflict' record and narrows the Maghway 2003 'non-stress language' remark to terminology (no phonemic stress; prominence predictable from length and H), not to a disagreement about where stress falls. Consistent with the earlier first reader's suggestion that the record should move from 'conflict' toward a weight-hedged coding (CVV penult, else final H, else initial) once Mous 1993 pp.21-27 are read directly.

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: all held-file parts of the composite quotation are verbatim at the stated locators (Downing 2004:108 with ex.4; Maghway 2003:51; Mous 2007:5; SPA 1979; Hyman 2006), but the deciding sentence attributed to Mous 1993:23 exists in our custody only as the StressTyp2 entry; the held Mous 1993 excerpts end at p.19. (2) Deciding source: a 1993 reference grammar (the best work on the language per Glottolog: Mous 1993, 363 pp; older alternatives Nordbustad 1988, Whiteley 1953/1958, Verhoeven 1926) but read second-hand; the opposing primary (Maghway 2003, journal article) is. Two independent carriers (StressTyp2 verbatim, Downing's paraphrase reproducing Mous's five examples) agree on the rule, so a mis-carry of the wording is unlikely; what is missing is Mous's context (relation of 'stress' to the H/L tone system, contrastiveness, closed syllables), and Mous's later statements w
audit.second_reader_evidence: The quotation was checked again: partly confirmed. Re-opened every held component at the stated locators and all are verbatim: Downing 2004 txt l.342-356 (rule paraphrase + ex.(4) ba/eeso, hlooro, mugul, wawitmo, basa; printed page number '108' at l.359); Maghway 2003 txt l.22-24 'Phonologically, Iraqw is a non-stress language. For syllable prosodic contrast, Iraqw relies upon pitch and duration instead. Iraqw is, therefore, a tone language'; Mous 2007 sketch l.206 'Tone: High, Low. High tone has a limited distribution (pitch accent)'; SPA 1979 l.384-391 ACCENT entry after Whiteley 1958; Hyman 2006 l.538-540 citing Mous 1993:21. The Mous 1993:23 sentence exists in custody only as the StressTyp2 entry

sources.quote: Iraqw, a South Cushitic language spoken in Tanzania, is described as having a very different sort of accent system, with quantity-sensitive stress, as well as tone (Mous 1993). High tones pattern with long vowels in attracting stress. As shown by the data in (4), below, the penult is stressed if it has a long vowel. (Not all words in this language are assigned High tone.)

sources.quote: Basically, words in Iraqw and Gorwaa carry one of two tone patterns: low level or falling (accent 1) or progredient (accent 2). Accent 2 is realized as a final high tone. [...] In the pre-Iraqwoid phase, syllable structure dictated a certain intonation pattern in the indicative mood, with high-pitched stress falling onto the penultimate syllable as long as it was heavy (CVV or CVVC). If it was light, however, low-pitched stress was fixed on the antepenultimate
sources.note: Describes Iraqw/Gorwaa synchronically as 'moderate tone or pitch accent languages' with a two-way accent-1/accent-2 contrast (final H = accent 2) and gives a historical (pre-Iraqwoid) weight-based stress pattern as the source of tonogenesis; no synchronic statement of where word stress falls in modern Iraqw, so silent on the catalog's rule.
